title: Indicators and methods for assessing acoustical preferences and needs of students in educational buildings: A review
central_proposition: This review proposes a comprehensive framework of occupant-related, dose-related, and building-related indicators and methods to systematically assess students' acoustical preferences and needs in educational buildings.

concept_definitions.name: Soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context

concept_definitions.name: Acoustical environment
concept_definitions.definition: a physical phenomenon that can be assessed by measuring dose-related indicators in terms of indoor acoustics such as SPL.

concept_definitions.name: Occupant-related indicators
concept_definitions.definition: Indicators related to human responses, categorized into physiological, psychological, and demographical aspects.

concept_definitions.name: Dose-related indicators
concept_definitions.definition: Indicators related to environmental stimuli, including acoustical parameters (e.g., sound pressure level) and other IEQ factors (e.g., temperature, illuminance).

concept_definitions.name: Building-related indicators
concept_definitions.definition: Indicators related to architectural features and building systems (e.g., sound absorbing walls, space layout, lighting type).

concept_definitions.name: Cross-modal perception
concept_definitions.definition: The perception of the interaction between two or more environmental stimuli such as between noise and temperature.

argument_structure: The paper synthesizes existing literature on indoor acoustics and soundscape studies, categorizing indicators into occupant-related, dose-related, and building-related. It then summarizes methods used to measure these indicators. Finally, it integrates this information into a comprehensive overview (Fig. 7) that illustrates the relationships between these indicator categories and methods for investigating students' acoustical preferences and needs in educational buildings.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The proposed framework posits that environmental stimuli (dose-related indicators) and building characteristics (building-related indicators) interact to influence human responses (occupant-related indicators), which encompass physiological and psychological needs and preferences. This interplay is often complex and cross-modal. By systematically measuring these indicators using appropriate methods, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of students' acoustical preferences and needs, thereby enabling the design of educational environments that promote well-being and performance.

findings.antecedent: Dose-related acoustical indicators (e.g., SPL, sound source)
findings.consequent: Students' physiological and psychological responses (e.g., stress, annoyance, cognitive performance)
findings.mechanism: Environmental acoustical stimuli directly impact human physiological systems (e.g., stress hormones, heart rate) and psychological states (e.g., annoyance, pleasantness, cognitive load), influencing well-being and task performance.
findings.quote: sound sources can have both physiological and psychological effects on students [20,33,39,84,85]. In addition, the SPL can adversely affect students' physiological needs [36,39].
findings.empirical_support_cited: [20,33,36,39,84,85] for physiological/psychological effects; [36,39] for SPL adversely affecting physiological needs; [47,48] for cognitive performance.

findings.antecedent: Building-related indicators (e.g., acoustical materials, space layout)
findings.consequent: Acoustical quality and students' occupant-related responses (physiological, psychological)
findings.mechanism: Architectural elements and building systems modify the propagation and characteristics of sound (dose-related indicators), which in turn affects students' physiological and psychological experiences, including their comfort and performance.
findings.quote: physical environment elements, such as the presence of acoustical walls and absorbing ceiling panels, can affect the acoustical quality in an indoor environment [17,49,55]. Additionally, space layout of an educational building can play a vital role in acoustical comfort [69].
findings.empirical_support_cited: [17,49,55] for physical elements affecting acoustical quality; [69] for space layout affecting acoustical comfort; [17,49,55,69] for interaction with occupant/dose-related indicators.

findings.antecedent: Cross-modal interactions between acoustical quality and other IEQ factors (e.g., thermal, lighting, visual scenes)
findings.consequent: Students' physiological and psychological responses (e.g., stress, annoyance, perception)
findings.mechanism: Sensory inputs from different environmental modalities are integrated, and the perception and impact of one modality (acoustics) can be altered by the conditions of another (e.g., visual scenes reducing noise annoyance, thermal conditions affecting acoustic perception).
findings.quote: students' physiological and psychological responses are associated with the combined effects of acoustical quality indicators (SPL and sound source) and thermal comfort indicators (temperature) [34,35,37,54,56].
findings.empirical_support_cited: [34,35,37,54,56] for physiological/psychological responses associated with combined acoustical and thermal indicators; [50-52] for cross-modal perception between acoustics and lighting/visual comfort; [51,77] for natural visual scenes reducing noise annoyance.

findings.antecedent: Comprehensive consideration of occupant-related, dose-related, and building-related indicators
findings.consequent: Effective assessment and optimization of indoor acoustics for students' preferences and needs
findings.mechanism: A holistic approach that integrates human responses, environmental stimuli, and architectural features provides a more complete understanding of the complex interplay, leading to better-tailored acoustical environments that meet diverse student needs and promote well-being and performance.
findings.quote: it is important to take into account all the three categories of indicators (occupant, environmental, and building) in order to assess the health and comfort of indoor environments.
findings.empirical_support_cited: it is important to take into account all the three categories of indicators (occupant, environmental, and building) in order to assess the health and comfort of indoor environments.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Applying the proposed comprehensive framework (integrating occupant-related, dose-related, and building-related indicators with appropriate methods) will lead to a more accurate understanding of students' acoustical preferences and needs in educational buildings compared to approaches focusing on only one or two indicator categories.

Interventions based on the comprehensive assessment of occupant-related, dose-related, and building-related indicators will result in improved student well-being and performance in educational settings.
bridge_warrants: The framework integrates human-centered approaches (soundscape) with objective environmental measurements, bridging subjective experience with physical parameters.
It highlights cross-modal interactions, connecting acoustics with thermal, lighting, and visual comfort frameworks.
It implicitly links to adaptive comfort theories by emphasizing individual preferences and needs and the dynamic nature of comfort.
methodological_critiques: Occupant-related indicators are rarely included in the acoustical performance guidelines of educational buildings.
Only a few previous studies investigated students' acoustical preferences and needs by considering occupant-related indicators (both physiological and psychological).
Dose-related indicators of other IEQ factors and building-related indicators were rarely taken into account in previous studies.
Soundwalk, as a method, was only applied in one study on a study environment in the reviewed literature.
Almost none of the reviewed studies explicitly considered students' acoustical preferences or needs in educational buildings.
model_structure: The paper proposes a three-part model (Fig. 7) comprising: 1) Inputs (Occupant-related, Dose-related, and Building-related indicators, each with subgroups); 2) Methods (Objective measurements at human/environmental levels, Soundwalk, Questionnaire, Interview, Binaural measurements, Playing sound stimuli, Building checklist/inspection); and 3) Outputs (Acoustical preferences and needs of students). The model suggests that systematic data collection on inputs using specified methods leads to a comprehensive understanding of outputs.
limitations: The review is limited to 44 selected studies.
The review is limited to studies on indoor acoustics and soundscape with regard to students in schools and universities (undergraduate and graduate), with a minimum age of 8 and maximum age of 34.
Soundwalk was only applied in one study on a study environment in the reviewed literature.
Almost none of the reviewed studies explicitly considered students' acoustical preferences or needs in educational buildings.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: As the rate and magnitude of climate change accelerate, understanding the consequences becomes increasingly important. Species distribution models (SDMs) based on current ecological niche constraints are used to project future species distributions. These models contain assumptions that add to the uncertainty in model projections stemming from the structure of the models, the algorithms used to translate niche associations into distributional probabilities, the quality and quantity of data, and mismatches between the scales of modeling and data. We illustrate the application of SDMs using two climate models and two distributional algorithms, together with information on distributional shifts in vegetation types, to project fine-scale future distributions of 60 California landbird species. Most species are projected to decrease in distribution by 2070. Changes in total species richness vary over the state, with large losses of species in some “hotspots” of vulnerability. Differences in distributional shifts among species will change species co-occurrences, creating spatial variation in similarities between current and future assemblages. We use these analyses to consider how assumptions can be addressed and uncertainties reduced. SDMs can provide a useful way to incorporate future conditions into conservation and management practices and decisions, but the uncertainties of model projections must be balanced with the risks of taking the wrong actions or the costs of inaction. Doing this will require that the sources and magnitudes of uncertainty are documented, and that conservationists and resource managers be willing to act despite the uncertainties. The alternative, of ignoring the future, is not an option.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper outlines a conceptual pathway from objective acoustical properties to subjective perceptions, cognitive demands, affective states, and ultimately, physiological and psychological outcomes in students within educational buildings.

steps.from_construct: Dose-related acoustical indicators (e.g., SPL, sound source characteristics)
steps.to_construct: Perception of the acoustical environment (e.g., loudness, clarity, intrusiveness)
Cognitive processing demands (e.g., effort to filter noise, distraction)

steps.from_construct: Affective responses and Cognitive processing demands
steps.to_construct: Physiological arousal (e.g., stress response) and Impaired cognitive performance (e.g., reduced attention, memory)
